title: Understanding APIs
text: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules and protocols that allows different software applications to communicate and exchange data with each other. One common way of simplifying this concept is to imagine you are in a restaurant. The end goal is get to be served the food from the kitchen. However, you cannot go directly to the kitchen to acquire food. Because of this, you (the client) must make an order through the waiter (the API) to be able to reach the kitchen (the server). The waiter will taker your order, verify your request, and return your food.

title: Understanding APIs
text:
Accessing Data
Learning how an API works is one thing, but it is important to note that there are many ways to set up an API. This means that while the general process for making a request is the same, the exact methods can vary. That said, there are five elements that make up essentially every API call:

URL

This is the server containing the data that are being targeted. This URL can be found in the API documentation provided by the company/service. To find the data desired, the client uses the base URL along with a specific endpoint that indicates which data the API should retrieve.

Method

Usually this is where something like the GET command is run, which tells the server you want to retrieve records hosted on the server.

Headers

These represent the metadata included in the request and response. They tell the server things like where the request originates and how to handle it.

Parameters

Items appended to the base URL that specify what data is being requested by the client.

Body (Payload)

The data sent from the server to the client, which is most commonly received in a JSON format.


As part of a previous class project, my team and I worked with the API provided by the UFA (Ultimate Frisbee Association). As seen in the image below, the UFA provides documentation about how the data are formatted, the base URL, and the endpoint.

Documentation like this is crucial to understanding not only how to request information, but how the data requested will be sent from the server.

title: Understanding APIs
text:
How Companies Use APIs
The purpose of an API for most companies goes far beyond allowing anyone to grab their data for a personal project. In reality, APIs have many different use cases. For example, they are critical for the operation of many businesses that leverage online payments. When a customer submits an order for a product, one or more API calls could be made. Examples of these are an API that processes payment, one that confirms the order, and another that updates a database.
It is also important to note the distinction between internal and external APIs. Internal APIs connect different parts of a company’s software, which allows them to communicate with each other. External APIs connect the company to another organization or user’s software. The UFA API mentioned above is a good example of an external API.

title: Understanding APIs
text:
Limitations and Restrictions
The ability to restrict who can access specific information through a specific API is simultaneously a great benefit and drawback. This is a benefit because sensitive information can be kept secure, while public or non-sensitive data can be made available to anyone with access to a machine capable of calling the API. Some of the most important restrictions to be aware of when working with APIs are rate and payload limits. Both are interrelated, but distinct.

Rate limit: a control that restricts the number of requests a user can make within a given timeframe.
Payload limit: a control that determines the maximum amount of data/records that can be sent in response to a request.

Being aware of these restrictions can help a client maintain access to an API along with a sustainable data pipeline.

title: Understanding APIs
text:
Tying It All Together
After having discussed some of the most important parts of APIs and how to work with them, below is an example of how a user could call an API from the website restcountries.com. The steps for doing so can be followed generally for many use cases, and should be helpful to continue working with APIs in a variety of ways.

import requests

# 1. Choose the API endpoint
url = "https://restcountries.com/v3.1/name/france"

# 2. Send a request to the API
response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)

# 3. Check whether the request succeeded
if response.status_code == 200:

    # 4. Convert the response into Python data
    countries = response.json()

    # 5. Extract and display the information we need
    country = countries[0]

    print("Country:", country["name"]["common"])
    print("Capital:", country["capital"][0])
    print("Population:", country["population"])

else:
    print("Request failed:", response.status_code)

title: Connecticut Sports Wagering Data Acquisition
text:
Motivating Question
What I do hope to discuss today is this: How has overall sports wagering spend changed since it was legalized? In this case, I looked at data provided by Connecticut Open Data, which dates back to late 2021, when online sports wagering became legal in the state. As someone who does not choose to participate in gambling myself, I realized I have my own biases and looked to find some data that could show me the real story. I originally sought out to see how gambling changed specifically for younger bettors, but had a difficult time finding that information. Additionally, that information might be a little more sensitive than aggregated totals for wagers across licensed operators in Connecticut.

title: Connecticut Sports Wagering Data Acquisition
text:
Ethical Data Collection
In the Connecticut Open Data terms of service, it explains how the organization reserves the right to modify and update data as it sees fit, but there is nothing that would preclude anyone from collecting and presenting the information found therein. After reading this, I determined it would be a viable option to work with this data.

title: Connecticut Sports Wagering Data Acquisition
text:
Acquisition Summary
Obtaining the data from the site is fairly straightforward. Here are the steps I used in order:

Navigate to the Connecticut Open Data Site
Find the dataset for which you would like to collect data
On the page displaying the dataset, click on “Actions”
Copy the API endpoint URL to your code
Use the get function via import requests to load the data onto your machine

While gambling metrics were of interest to me, this process can be followed for a large variety of topics on the site to access the information.

title: Connecticut Sports Wagering Data Acquisition
text:
EDA Highlights
As I was exploring the data, I discovered that the measurements for 2021 were often much smaller than future years. After some digging I found that wagers were only recorded in October, November, and December of that year. Because of this, that year was dropped from most of my analysis. Similarly, since I am writing this at the beginning of November 2026, that year is not yet over. However, I felt it would be more interesting to see the aggregations so far and see how they compare. Below are some of my insights.

As you can see, online sports wagering as a whole has continued to increase since its legalization, and it is by no small margin. We will see in coming days whether the trend continues through 2026.


Wagers and Winnings

I found this graph to be insightful, as it shows that even as total wagers increase, the total winnings awarded remain below the amount wagered. While sports betting may seem like there are different odds and more skill involved, the data tells us that the house most certainly always wins.

title: Connecticut Sports Wagering Data Acquisition
text:
Conclusion
If you are interested in exploring the Connecticut Open Data portal, you can check out the site at data.ct.gov. The website is very user friendly and has plenty of things to explore. If the topic of gambling itself interests you, one site I found allows users to easily explore data comes from The University of Indiana and their 2024 Adult Gambling Behaviors in Idiana Survey. It allows the user to create custom visualizations based on a number of gambling categories.
